## `virtualization.cluster.host.count`

| Name | Instrument Type | Unit (UCUM) | Description | Stability | Entity Associations |
| -------- | --------------- | ----------- | -------------- | --------- | ------ |
| `virtualization.cluster.host.count` | UpDownCounter | `{host}` | The number of physical hosts or hypervisor nodes currently members of the virtualization cluster. [1] | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `virtualization.cluster` |

**Requirement Level:** `Recommended`

**[1]:** Reports the active node membership of the compute cluster. In VMware vSphere, this corresponds to `cluster.numHosts` on the ClusterComputeResource summary. In KVM management clusters (e.g., oVirt or Proxmox VE), this represents the total active member nodes. In OpenShift Virtualization (KubeVirt), this corresponds to the count of schedulable worker nodes hosting VM workloads (`kubevirt_cluster_nodes`).

**Attributes:**

| Key | Stability | [Requirement Level](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/general/attribute-requirement-level/) | Value Type | Description | Example Values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `virtualization.cluster.name` | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `Required` | string | The human-readable name assigned to the virtualization cluster. [1] | `prod-cluster-01`; `us-east-zone-a` |
| `virtualization.cluster.id` | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `Recommended` | string | Unique identifier for the virtualization cluster. [2] | `cluster-001`; `8c3f2a1b-4d56-4e78-9f01-2a3b4c5d6e7f` |
| `virtualization.system.name` | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `Recommended` | string | The name of the virtualization system (hypervisor technology) managing this platform. [3] | `ibm.prsm`; `ibm.zvm`; `ibm.powervm` |

**[1] `virtualization.cluster.name`:** The name as configured in the cluster management interface. For VMware vSphere this is the cluster name shown in vCenter. For IBM Z HMC multi-CPC management domains this corresponds to the HMC ensemble or management domain name.

**[2] `virtualization.cluster.id`:** The opaque identifier of the cluster.

**[3] `virtualization.system.name`:** Identifies the virtualization technology managing this cluster.

## `virtualization.hypervisor.memory.overcommit_ratio`

| Name | Instrument Type | Unit (UCUM) | Description | Stability | Entity Associations |
| -------- | --------------- | ----------- | -------------- | --------- | ------ |
| `virtualization.hypervisor.memory.overcommit_ratio` | Gauge | `1` | The ratio of total virtual machine memory allocations to physical host memory on the hypervisor. [3] | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `virtualization.hypervisor` |

**Requirement Level:** `Recommended`

**[3]:** Calculated as the sum of all configured or granted virtual machine memory limits divided by the total usable physical RAM of the hypervisor host. A value greater than 1.0 indicates memory overcommitment (e.g., 1.5 indicates 150% committed). In VMware vCenter, this represents the Host Memory Overcommit ratio. In KVM (libvirt), it corresponds to `sum(domain_max_memory) / node_memory_total`. In OpenShift Virtualization (KubeVirt), this maps to `kubevirt_node_memory_overcommit_ratio`.

**Attributes:**

| Key | Stability | [Requirement Level](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/general/attribute-requirement-level/) | Value Type | Description | Example Values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `virtualization.hypervisor.id` | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `Required` | string | Unique identifier for the hypervisor instance. [8] | `8c3f2a1b-4d56-4e78-9f01-2a3b4c5d6e7f` |
| `virtualization.system.name` | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `Recommended` | string | The name of the virtualization system (hypervisor technology) managing this platform. [9] | `ibm.prsm`; `ibm.zvm`; `ibm.powervm` |

**[8] `virtualization.hypervisor.id`:** A UUID or other platform-specific opaque identifier that uniquely identifies this hypervisor instance within the virtualization platform.

**[9] `virtualization.system.name`:** Identifies the virtualization technology managing this hypervisor.

## `virtualization.partition.cpu.count`

| Name | Instrument Type | Unit (UCUM) | Description | Stability | Entity Associations |
| -------- | --------------- | ----------- | -------------- | --------- | ------ |
| `virtualization.partition.cpu.count` | UpDownCounter | `{vcpu}` | The number of virtual processors of the specified type currently allocated to the firmware partition. [4] | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `virtualization.partition` |

**Requirement Level:** `Recommended`

**[4]:** Reports the current virtual processor allocation for the partition. In IBM Z PR/SM (classic mode) this maps to the processor-count-* fields on the logical-partition or partition object in the HMC Web Services API. Analogous to `mainframe.partition.cpu.virtual.count` in the mainframe namespace.

**Attributes:**

| Key | Stability | [Requirement Level](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/general/attribute-requirement-level/) | Value Type | Description | Example Values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `virtualization.partition.id` | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `Required` | string | Unique identifier for the hardware or firmware partition. [10] | `0abc1234-5678-90ab-cdef-1234567890ab`; `partition-3` |
| `virtualization.partition.cpu.type` | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `Recommended` | string | The category of processor type allocated to the firmware partition. [11] | `cp`; `ifl`; `icf` |

**[10] `virtualization.partition.id`:** A platform-specific opaque identifier that uniquely identifies this partition within its virtualization platform. On IBM Z in PR/SM (classic) mode this is the partition object-id assigned by the HMC.

**[11] `virtualization.partition.cpu.type`:** Identifies the processor type being counted. Use `all` for the total count across all processor types.

## `virtualization.partition.cpu.is_capped`

| Name | Instrument Type | Unit (UCUM) | Description | Stability | Entity Associations |
| -------- | --------------- | ----------- | -------------- | --------- | ------ |
| `virtualization.partition.cpu.is_capped` | Gauge | `1` | Indicates whether processor capping is enabled for the firmware partition (0=false, 1=true). [5] | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `virtualization.partition` |

**Requirement Level:** `Recommended`

**[5]:** When capping is enabled the partition cannot exceed its allocated processor count or scheduling weight ceiling regardless of spare capacity on the platform. In IBM Z PR/SM this corresponds to the `is-processing-weight-capped` field on the logical-partition or partition object in the HMC Web Services API (all modes). Equivalent concepts exist on VMware vSphere (CPU limit), KVM (cputune quota), and Hyper-V (processor bandwidth limits).

## `virtualization.partition.cpu.weight`

| Name | Instrument Type | Unit (UCUM) | Description | Stability | Entity Associations |

**Requirement Level:** `Recommended`

**[8]:** The weight determines the proportion of available processor cycles allocated to this partition relative to other partitions when spare capacity is available. Higher weights grant proportionally more CPU time under contention. In IBM Z PR/SM the weight is an integer in the range 1–999 set on the logical partition or partition object via the HMC Web Services API properties `initial-processing-weight`, `minimum-processing-weight`, `current-processing-weight`, and `maximum-processing-weight` (all modes). Use the `mainframe.partition.weight.type` attribute to discriminate between weight categories on IBM Z; omit on platforms that do not expose multiple weight categories.

| Key | Stability | [Requirement Level](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/general/attribute-requirement-level/) | Value Type | Description | Example Values |

| `mainframe.partition.weight.type` | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `Opt-In` | string | The scheduling weight type that determines how processor time is allocated to the logical partition (LPAR). [18] | `initial`; `minimum`; `current` |

**[17] `virtualization.partition.id`:** A platform-specific opaque identifier that uniquely identifies this partition within its virtualization platform. On IBM Z in PR/SM (classic) mode this is the partition object-id assigned by the HMC.

**[18] `mainframe.partition.weight.type`:** IBM Z–specific. Identifies the weight category being reported (initial, minimum, current, or maximum). Omit on platforms that do not differentiate processing weight by category.

`mainframe.partition.weight.type` has the following list of well-known values. If one of them applies, then the respective value MUST be used; otherwise, a custom value MAY be used.

| Value | Description | Stability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `current` | The current processor weight actively in use by the partition at the time of observation. | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) |
| `initial` | The initial processor weight assigned to the partition at activation, representing its baseline entitlement. | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) |
| `maximum` | The maximum processor weight the partition may consume when spare capacity is available. | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) |
| `minimum` | The minimum processor weight guaranteed to the partition, below which its allocation will not fall. | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) |

## `virtualization.partition.state.code`

| Name | Instrument Type | Unit (UCUM) | Description | Stability | Entity Associations |

| `virtualization.partition.state.code` | Gauge | `1` | The operational state of the firmware partition encoded as a numeric gauge (1=in this state, 0=not in this state). [10] | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `virtualization.partition` |

**[10]:** Reports the current lifecycle state of the partition. For each partition, exactly one state value will be 1 at any given time; all others will be 0. Valid state values are defined by the `virtualization.partition.state` attribute enum (active, not_activated, stopped, unknown). Analogous to `mainframe.partition.status.code` in the mainframe namespace.

## `virtualization.vm.cpu.ready_time`

| Name | Instrument Type | Unit (UCUM) | Description | Stability | Entity Associations |
| -------- | --------------- | ----------- | -------------- | --------- | ------ |
| `virtualization.vm.cpu.ready_time` | Counter | `s` | The cumulative time the virtual machine's virtual CPUs (vCPUs) were ready to run but waiting for physical CPU time from the hypervisor. [22] | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `virtualization.vm` |

**Requirement Level:** `Recommended`

**[22]:** Measures hypervisor scheduling contention from the guest's perspective. High ready time indicates the physical host is overcommitted and vCPUs are competing for physical CPU time. In IBM z/VM this corresponds to the dispatch wait time per guest. In VMware ESXi it corresponds to the cpu.ready.summation counter converted from milliseconds to seconds. In Microsoft Hyper-V it corresponds to "% Hypervisor Run Time" on the Hyper-V Virtual Processor object. Not directly available in IBM Z PR/SM (classic mode) — implementations may omit this metric on that platform.

## `virtualization.vm.cpu.steal_time`

| Name | Instrument Type | Unit (UCUM) | Description | Stability | Entity Associations |
| -------- | --------------- | ----------- | -------------- | --------- | ------ |
| `virtualization.vm.cpu.steal_time` | Counter | `s` | The cumulative time the virtual machine's virtual CPUs (vCPUs) were runnable but could not execute because the hypervisor was running other guests. [23] | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `virtualization.vm` |

**Requirement Level:** `Recommended`

**[23]:** CPU steal time quantifies the scheduling overhead imposed by the hypervisor on this VM. A high steal time indicates the physical host is overcommitted and the hypervisor is not honouring the VM's CPU allocations. This is distinct from `virtualization.vm.cpu.ready_time` which measures time waiting in the scheduler queue. In KVM (libvirt) environments it corresponds to the steal_time field from virDomainGetCPUStats(), converted from nanoseconds to seconds. In OpenShift Virtualization (KubeVirt) it corresponds to the kubevirt_vmi_vcpu_wait_seconds_total counter. Not available on IBM Z PR/SM (classic mode), IBM z/VM, VMware ESXi, or Microsoft Hyper-V — implementations on those platforms should omit this metric.

**Attributes:**

| Key | Stability | [Requirement Level](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/general/attribute-requirement-level/) | Value Type | Description | Example Values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `virtualization.vm.id` | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `Required` | string | Unique identifier for the virtual machine instance. [44] | `vm-0abc1234`; `8c3f2a1b-4d56-4e78-9f01-2a3b4c5d6e7f` |
| `virtualization.vm.node.name` | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `Recommended` | string | The name of the host node on which the virtual machine is currently scheduled to run. [45] | `worker-node-01`; `compute-az1-007`; `rhcos-node-03` |

**[44] `virtualization.vm.id`:** A UUID or other platform-specific opaque identifier that uniquely identifies this virtual machine within the hypervisor. Analogous to `host.id` for physical machines or a container ID for containers.

**[45] `virtualization.vm.node.name`:** The Kubernetes node (or KVM host) on which the VM is running. High steal time on one node may indicate host overcommitment specific to that node's physical CPU count.

## `virtualization.vm.cpu.utilization`

| Name | Instrument Type | Unit (UCUM) | Description | Stability | Entity Associations |
| -------- | --------------- | ----------- | -------------- | --------- | ------ |
| `virtualization.vm.cpu.utilization` | Gauge | `1` | The fraction of time the virtual machine's virtual CPUs (vCPUs) were busy executing work, as a ratio from 0 (idle) to 1 (fully utilised). [24] | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `virtualization.vm` |

**Requirement Level:** `Recommended`

**[24]:** Measures active execution time from the guest's perspective, aggregated across all vCPUs. In IBM Z PR/SM (classic mode) this maps to the processor-usage fields in the logical-partition-usage metric group via the HMC Web Services API. In IBM z/VM it corresponds to CP usage per guest virtual machine. In VMware ESXi it corresponds to the cpu.usage.average performance counter. In Microsoft Hyper-V it corresponds to the "% Total Run Time" counter on the Hyper-V Virtual Processor object. In KVM (libvirt) environments it corresponds to the cpu_time field from the virDomainGetCPUStats() API, converted to a ratio by dividing by (elapsed_ns × vCPU_count). In OpenShift Virtualization (KubeVirt) it corresponds to the kubevirt_vmi_cpu_usage_seconds_total counter, rate-converted to a ratio. A value of 1 means all vCPUs were 100% busy during the measurement interval.

## `virtualization.vm.disk.latency.time`

| Name | Instrument Type | Unit (UCUM) | Description | Stability | Entity Associations |
| -------- | --------------- | ----------- | -------------- | --------- | ------ |
| `virtualization.vm.disk.latency.time` | Counter | `s` | Total time spent waiting for virtual disk I/O operations to complete in seconds. [27] | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `virtualization.vm` |

**Requirement Level:** `Recommended`

**[27]:** A monotonically increasing counter measuring cumulative time spent by the hypervisor and backing storage stack processing guest read and write operations. When divided by the delta of `virtualization.vm.disk.operations` over the same interval, it yields average round-trip I/O latency in seconds per operation. In VMware ESXi, this maps to `disk.totalReadLatency.average` and `disk.totalWriteLatency.average` (accumulated). In KVM (libvirt), this corresponds to virDomainBlockStats read_time and write_time fields (libvirt_domain_block_stats_read_time_seconds_total). In OpenShift Virtualization (KubeVirt), this maps to kubevirt_vmi_storage_read_times_ms_total and write_times_ms_total converted from milliseconds to seconds.

## `virtualization.vm.memory.allocated`

| Name | Instrument Type | Unit (UCUM) | Description | Stability | Entity Associations |
| -------- | --------------- | ----------- | -------------- | --------- | ------ |
| `virtualization.vm.memory.allocated` | Gauge | `MiBy` | The total amount of memory currently allocated to the virtual machine by the hypervisor, in mebibytes (MiB). [29] | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `virtualization.vm` |

**Requirement Level:** `Recommended`

**[29]:** Reports the memory allocation as seen by the hypervisor — the amount committed to this VM regardless of what the guest OS is actively using. In IBM Z PR/SM (classic mode) this corresponds to the initial-memory or current central storage allocation on the partition object via the HMC Web Services API. In IBM z/VM it is the real storage assigned to the guest. In VMware ESXi it corresponds to mem.granted.average converted from kilobytes to mebibytes. In Microsoft Hyper-V it is the physical memory assigned as reported by Dynamic Memory or static configuration.

## `virtualization.vm.memory.balloon`

| Name | Instrument Type | Unit (UCUM) | Description | Stability | Entity Associations |
| -------- | --------------- | ----------- | -------------- | --------- | ------ |
| `virtualization.vm.memory.balloon` | Gauge | `MiBy` | The amount of memory reclaimed from the virtual machine by the hypervisor's memory ballooning mechanism, in mebibytes (MiB). [30] | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `virtualization.vm` |

**Requirement Level:** `Recommended`

**[30]:** Memory ballooning is a technique where the hypervisor inflates a balloon driver inside the guest OS to reclaim memory under host pressure. A non-zero value indicates the hypervisor is reclaiming memory from this VM. In VMware ESXi this corresponds to mem.vmmemctl.average converted from kilobytes to mebibytes. In Microsoft Hyper-V it relates to memory pressure adjustments via the Dynamic Memory mechanism. Not applicable on IBM Z PR/SM or IBM z/VM — implementations on those platforms should omit this metric or report 0.

## `virtualization.vm.memory.rss`

| Name | Instrument Type | Unit (UCUM) | Description | Stability | Entity Associations |
| -------- | --------------- | ----------- | -------------- | --------- | ------ |
| `virtualization.vm.memory.rss` | Gauge | `MiBy` | The amount of physical host memory (resident set size) currently mapped to the virtual machine's address space, in mebibytes (MiB). [31] | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `virtualization.vm` |

**Requirement Level:** `Recommended`

**[31]:** Resident Set Size (RSS) reports the actual physical host memory pages that back the VM at a given moment. Unlike `virtualization.vm.memory.allocated` (which reflects the configured allocation), RSS reflects real consumption accounting for memory ballooning, KSM (Kernel Same-page Merging), and huge page backing. A VM with high allocated memory but low RSS is not causing physical memory pressure. In KVM (libvirt) environments it corresponds to the rss field from the memory.stat output of virDomainMemoryStats(), converted from kilobytes to mebibytes. In OpenShift Virtualization (KubeVirt) it corresponds to the kubevirt_vmi_memory_resident_bytes metric (converted from bytes to MiB). Not directly available on IBM Z PR/SM, IBM z/VM, VMware ESXi, or Microsoft Hyper-V — implementations on those platforms should omit this metric or approximate it using `virtualization.vm.memory.used`.

**[58] `virtualization.vm.node.name`:** The Kubernetes node (or KVM host) on which the VM is running. Useful for correlating RSS with per-node NUMA memory topology.

## `virtualization.vm.network.io`

| Name | Instrument Type | Unit (UCUM) | Description | Stability | Entity Associations |

**[34]:** A monotonically increasing counter of bytes transferred through the virtual network interface since the VM started or the counter last reset. The direction (receive or transmit) is carried by the `network.io.direction` attribute. Use rate() in Prometheus or equivalent to derive throughput in bytes per second. In Microsoft Hyper-V it corresponds to the "Bytes Received/sec" and "Bytes Sent/sec" counters on the Hyper-V Virtual Network Adapter object, accumulated as a counter.

## `virtualization.vm.power.state`

| Name | Instrument Type | Unit (UCUM) | Description | Stability | Entity Associations |
| -------- | --------------- | ----------- | -------------- | --------- | ------ |
| `virtualization.vm.power.state` | Gauge | `1` | The current power state of the virtual machine encoded as a numeric gauge (1=in this state, 0=not in this state). [35] | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) | `virtualization.vm` |

**Requirement Level:** `Recommended`

**[35]:** Reports the operational lifecycle state of the VM as a dimensioned gauge. For each VM, exactly one state value will be 1 at any given time; all others will be 0. This encoding enables Prometheus alerting rules and state-change detection without label-value cardinality issues. In IBM Z PR/SM (classic mode) this maps to the partition status field on the logical-partition object via the HMC Web Services API. In IBM z/VM it maps to guest state. In VMware ESXi it maps to runtime.powerState. In Microsoft Hyper-V it maps to the VM operational state property.

`virtualization.vm.state` has the following list of well-known values. If one of them applies, then the respective value MUST be used; otherwise, a custom value MAY be used.

| Value | Description | Stability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `failed` | Virtual machine has encountered a fatal error and cannot recover without operator intervention. | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) |
| `migrating` | Virtual machine is being live-migrated to another host without interruption. | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) |
| `paused` | Virtual machine is suspended with state preserved in memory. | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) |
| `running` | Virtual machine is running and processing workloads. | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) |
| `scheduled` | Virtual machine has been assigned to a host node and is being prepared to start. | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) |
| `scheduling` | Virtual machine has been requested but is waiting for the scheduler to assign it to a host node. | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) |
| `stopped` | Virtual machine is stopped and not consuming CPU resources. | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) |
| `succeeded` | Virtual machine completed its workload and terminated cleanly (applicable to batch or ephemeral VMs). | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) |
| `unknown` | Virtual machine state is not known or cannot be determined. | ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue) |
